scenes.title: Debugging & Troubleshooting from the Terminal
scenes.narration: When a pipeline breaks on a remote server, the terminal is where you diagnose the problem and get things running again.

scenes.title: A Debugging Mindset
bullets: Read the error message and traceback carefully — it usually names the real cause.
Reproduce the failure reliably before you attempt any fix.
Change one thing at a time so you know what actually resolved it.
Check logs, resources, and the environment, not just the code.
scenes.narration: Effective debugging begins with actually reading the traceback, which most often points straight at the culprit. Before fixing anything, make the bug reproducible so you can confirm progress. Change a single variable at a time to avoid confusing yourself about what worked. And remember that the problem may lie in logs, disk space, or environment variables rather than the code itself.

scenes.title: Terminal Troubleshooting Toolkit
scenes.code:
tail -f /var/log/etl.log     # watch live logs
df -h                        # disk space
free -h                      # memory usage
ps aux | grep python         # is it running?
curl -I https://api.site.com # can I reach it?
scenes.narration: This toolkit covers the usual suspects. Following the log reveals what the job is doing in real time, while df and free check whether you have run out of disk or memory. Grepping the process list confirms whether the program is even alive, and a curl request tests connectivity to an external service. Together they quickly localize where a failure lives.

scenes.title: Dropping Into a Python Debugger
scenes.code:
def transform(row):
    import pdb; pdb.set_trace()  # pause here
    cleaned = row.strip().lower()
    return cleaned
scenes.narration: For logic bugs, Python's built-in debugger is invaluable. Inserting pdb.set_trace pauses execution at that exact line and gives you an interactive prompt. From there you can inspect variables, step through the code, and watch exactly how the data flows, which turns guessing into observing.

scenes.text: Read the error first, reproduce it, then change one thing at a time — disciplined debugging beats random guessing every time.
scenes.narration: A calm, systematic approach almost always wins. Read the error, reproduce it reliably, and isolate changes one at a time instead of poking around at random.
